objects: multivariate regression; cross-phenotype effect sharing; prior families
assumptions: multiple phenotypes with complex effect-size distributions
conclusion: Existing multivariate Bayesian regression priors are relatively inflexible and their MCMC fitting can be impractical at genome-wide scale.
scope: Author-stated motivation; no universal comparison theorem.
span: However, despite the added flexibility compared to the MLMM model, the prior families used in existing multivariate Bayesian methods make them relatively inflexible to cope with the complex distribution of effect sizes that many complex traits have. In fact, most of those methods either have a single distribution or a “spike-and-slab” type of prior, with only one non-point-mass (“slab”) component. In addition, the use of computationally intensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms for model fitting makes the multivariate Bayesian alphabet methods impractical in many “genome-wide” settings, even with a moderate number of phenotypes.

objects: S0 covariance collection; w0 mixture weights
assumptions: chosen covariance collection spans candidate sharing patterns
conclusion: Prior covariance matrices are prespecified while their mixture weights are estimated from the data.
scope: Covariance selection is a degree of freedom rather than a sampling assumption.
span: Following [35], we assume that the covariance matrices S_{0} are pre-specified, and treat the mixture weights w0 as parameters to be estimated from the data. The idea is that the collection of matrices S_{0} should be chosen to include a wide variety of potential effect sharing patterns; the estimated w0 should then assign most weight to the sharing patterns that are present in the data and little or no weight to patterns that are inconsistent with the data.

objects: w0; V; approximate marginal likelihood; ELBO
conclusion: Model parameters w0 and V are estimated by maximizing the evidence lower bound as an approximation to the marginal likelihood.
scope: Approximate marginal-likelihood fitting, not exact empirical Bayes optimization.
span: In addition to approximating the posterior distribution of B, the variational approach also provides a way to estimate the model parameters, w0 and V, by maximizing an approximation to the marginal likelihood, p ( Y ∣ X , V , w_{0} , S_{0} ), which is known as the “evidence lower bound” (ELBO) [48]. This approach was called “variational empirical Bayes” in [51], although this idea of fitting the model parameters by maximizing an approximate marginal likelihood dates back to earlier work [52, 53].

assumptions: missing outcome entries and current intercept, effect and covariance estimates
conclusion: Missing outcomes are handled by extending the variational approximation to their posterior and adding an imputation step.
scope: Missing Y values; no extension to missing predictors stated here.
span: To deal with missing values, we extend the variational approximation to include the posterior distribution of the missing entries (see the S1 Text for details). Computationally, this extension adds a step to the iterative algorithm that “imputes” the missing values. Specifically, denoting Yobs as the set of observed expression levels and Ymiss as the set of unobserved (missing) expression levels, the approach imputes the missing values Ymiss by computing an approximate posterior distribution for Ymiss given Yobs and current estimates of the intercept b0, effects B, and residual covariance V.

span: The trade-off is that the approximate posterior distribution obtained with our variational methods will tend to overstate certainty compared with the true posterior distribution [48], and so its use for inference (as opposed to prediction) requires particular care [20].

objects: correlated predictors; posterior dependence; variable selection
assumptions: two predictors perfectly correlated and one causal in the stated example
conclusion: The variational approximation cannot represent strong effect dependence and may select one perfectly correlated predictor at random while excluding the other, a behavior also attributed to the Lasso.
scope: Variable selection limitation; the authors distinguish this from prediction accuracy.
span: This is because the variational approximation used in mr.mash cannot capture the strong dependence in the posterior distribution for the effects of highly correlated variables. Indeed, if two variables are perfectly correlated, and one is causal, mr.mash will select one at random and exclude the other [20]. (This behavior is also displayed by the Lasso [41].)
